I run many data analysis projects as a hobbyist. I've been involved as an analyst in several online and esport communities, where I've analyzed player and team performances and metrics.

Hi! My name is Sin.
I’m a multidisciplinary biologist.

 



          
I offer several flavors of personal introduction. The choice is yours!



BriefElevator pitchDeeper diveAcademiaIndustry-speakGeoTrailPictographic


Former scientist, doctoral researcher and graduate at MPICE, IMPRS and Friedrich Schiller University with five published articles on molecular profiling, cell biology and neuroscience of Drosophila sensory systems.
Educated and trained prior at Utrecht University across a broad range of life-science projects involving fungi, (epi)genomics, molecular chaperones, microtubule dynamics, nanobodies, biomolecular docking and biotech applications.
Check out my research output and CV! If you enjoy tl;dr and BLUF practices, see my tl;dr page.


Hello there! I’m a biologist with diverse, international research lab experiences and broad technical training. I thrive on multidisciplinary projects and enjoy tackling complex questions through combined experimental-computational approaches. My past research interests span molecular biology, neuroscience, chemical ecology, animal behavior, genome biology, cytology, microbe physiology and data science. I’m comfortable navigating between biological disciplines, bring new perspective and rigor, and strive for inventive, original output.
Professionally, I’ve worked most recently on the molecular cell biology & neuroscience of olfaction at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology (dept. Evolutionary Neuroethology). I’ve worked in university, institute and hospital environments, and involve myself actively in various projects, often involving science communication, teaching, community organization and media production. For a little overview, see my complete CV.
My research portfolio consists of scientific publications in expert journals and a variety of presentations given at specialist conferences across the world. I keep a complete list of exemplary articles, preprints, posters and talks I’ve delivered on the research output page.
I’m versatile and like many things. Check some out on my random little tidbit gallery.


I’m a versatile PhD-graduate biologist with extensive international lab and life experience, cross-disciplinary expertise and a portfolio of publications in scientific journals and talks at international specialist conferences. My career has unfolded many disciplines, organisms, and research cultures. My scientific path has taken me through molecular cell biology, sensory neuroscience, ecology, genome biology, and computational analysis, often weaving these threads together in multidisciplinary projects.
I enjoy moving between fields, learning new techniques quickly, and building bridges between experimental and analytical perspectives. This breadth has given me a strong foundation in both wet-lab experimentation and data-driven inquiry, as well as an appreciation for how different scientific traditions approach the same biological questions. I feel like I have a lot to offer.
Trained chiefly in molecular cell biology and neuroscience, I now have over a decade of experience in various life science research labs, including university, institute and hospital environments. I’m comfortable navigating between biological disciplines, and personally strive for inventive and original output. My work always reflects this ethic and cross-disciplinarity.
So far, it has spanned areas like molecular biology and bioinformatics, cytology, ecology, sensory neuroscience, genome biology, epigenetics, molecular technique development, animal behavior, microbe physiology and evolution.
In addition to having spent many years planning and running experiments in labs, I’ve led and managed research projects (independently and collaboratively), frequently worked with large -omics and multidimensional datasets, involved myself in conference organization, colleague representation, university course teaching and student supervision, designed and tested novel biological probes, written many scripts for data analysis, all the while writing and illustrating and enjoying getting technical ideas across with clarity and elegance.
In short, I enjoy contributing to environments where interdisciplinary thinking and approach are valued and increasingly necessary. I relish in learning, trying things for their own sake, and applying my breadth of experience to find progress in new contexts.


I am a published multidisciplinary biologist with over a decade of academic research experience spanning molecular cell biology, sensory neuroscience, ecology, genome biology, cytology, epigenetics, bioinformatics, microbe physiology, evolution and animal behavior. My work integrates experimental and computational approaches. I have trained in multiple international laboratories, gaining broad methodological expertise and a strong foundation in both hypothesis-driven experimentation and quantitative analysis, as well as scientific writing and presentation.
Much of my formal research output is focused on the sensory biology and chemical ecology of insects. Chiefly, I’ve worked in olfactory neuroscience using Drosophila vinegar flies as a tractable model system. I’ve investigated and demonstrated the involvement of V-ATPase proton pumps, innexin gap junctions and hemichannels, nitric oxide and cGMP signaling, and non-neuronal support cell activity within the Drosophila antenna.
My doctoral dissertation unifies much of my work at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology and serves as an extensive treatise on insect olfaction. It also suggests future directions for research in emerging fields focusing on non-neuronal cell functions in compartmentalized systems. The authoring of a review concerning non-neuronal contributions to sensory systems is currently in progress.
Aside from this, I’ve also gathered experiences from major research projects:

In a cellular dynamics lab, I studied angiogenesis using human endothelial spheroid and organoid models and determined roles of microtubule-organizing genes and organelles in blood vessel outgrowth.
In a translational immunology lab, I adapted novel molecular techniques for massively parallel identification and quantification of DNA regulatory element activity across the human genome. Experiences included ChIP-seq, DNase-seq, STARR-seq and luciferase assays.
In a fungal physiology lab, I profiled growth and saccharification capacities of thermophilic fungi, comparing their ability to degrade plant biomass relevant to advanced biofuel production.

I also completed several laboratory rotations involving extracellular chaperones, nanobody technologies and biomolecular docking simulations.
Going forward, I am particularly interested in complex biological systems and questions, cross-disciplinary research, combinations of computational and experimental biology, and unearthing molecular mechanisms with native organismal functions and behaviors.


I’m a versatile biologist with hands-on experience in molecular and cellular biology, neuroscience, and data-driven hypothesis testing and computational analysis. I’ve worked in fast-paced international research environments where adaptability, technical breadth, and cross-functional collaboration were essential.
My background includes bioinformatics, assay development, familiarity with a wide range of light microscopic techniques, genome-scale analysis and (electro)physiology.
I’m comfortable writing technically, navigating complex datasets, troubleshooting experimental workflows, and contributing to multidisciplinary teams, systems and projects with fine-grained attentiveness to detail and specific demand.
I bring a strong foundation in hypothesis-driven experimentation, quantitative analysis, methodological expertise and a practical, solution-oriented mindset. I love working in dynamic teams, and communicating insights with expert and non-expert colleagues, audiences and clients in tailored manners.


Born in Yugoslavia.
Raised young in Serbia and then Poland.
Moved to Prague, Czech Republic as a child, attending a British international school.
As an adolescent I’ve been lucky to travel to Denmark, Slovenia, Croatia, Hungary, Slovakia and Austria.
Moved to the Netherlands as young adult. There I obtained BSc and MSc degrees at Utrecht University.
Moved back to Prague for a few years, involving myself in local art communities and working on many creative projects and side gigs.
Then moved to Jena, Germany to pursue doctoral research in molecular biology/neuroscience at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology.
The stint involved many international conference travels and research visits, including Kenya, Tanzania, Portugal, France and various campuses/cities around Germany.
Currently traveling between cities and countrysides all over Europe. Recent trips include the UK, Belgium, Netherlands, Poland, Czech Republic and Germany.
Where to next? Who can tell…

Publications

As lead author:







 





Expression of Drosophila melanogaster V-ATPases in olfactory sensillum support cells.


Prelic, Jain et al.


Published in Insects journal in 2024.


Link Supplementary data (FigShare)








NoteSummary(Research Article: 13 pages, 7 figures)






We perform bioinformatic analyses and immunofluorescence microscopy to explore and then pinpoint the expression of proton pumps in the fruit fly olfactory system. We hypothesize such pumps are situated on non-neuronal cells, and are involved in the critical regulation of proton and K+ concentrations necessary for correct sensory functioning.


We discover abundant expression of many genes composing the proton pump family in Drosophila antennae, and further localize these to support cells of antennal sensilla by analysis of cell type classes in single-cell transcriptomes, as well as showing their localization via immunolabeling in antennal sections. We demonstrate and further discuss mechanisms by which extracellular ionic compositions are maintained, and how known proton/K+ antiporters may then facilitate sensory function in animals.
















 





Non-canonical sensory biology of antennal cells in insect olfaction.


Prelic, S.


Published in Thuringian University & State Library (ThULB) in 2024.


Link








NoteSummary(Dissertation: 261 pages, 13 figures, 3 embedded manuscripts)






I identify and review non-neuronal processes and constituents of olfactory organs as crucial (though under-explored) elements of insect olfactory systems. I then set out to investigate several ‘non-canonical’ mechanisms in insect antennae, an area that remains entirely unexplored. I present original research articles on:




intercellular interactions between neuronal and non-neuronal cells. I demonstrate coupled activity between these cell types during sensory activity,


paracrine signaling (messenger-mediated cell-cell communication), exploring signaling pathways and their effects on potentiating sensory processes,


juxtacrine signaling (contact-dependent communication), showing the presence of gap junctions within insect olfactory organs.




Given this budding subject and field of research, I also propose a wide range of novel considerations, hypotheses and practical research directions for future exploration of animal sensory systems, especially given notable (though unreported) parallels among various sensory systems.
















 





Innexin expression and localization in the Drosophila antenna indicate gap junction or hemichannel involvement in antennal chemosensory sensilla.


Prelic et al.


Published in Cell and Tissue Research in 2024.


Link Supplementary data








NoteSummary(Research Article: 28 pages, 7 figures, 4 supplementary figures)






Olfactory system structures are highly conserved, with sensory neurons and adjacent cells closely apositioned, forming tight and encosed compartments. Whether gap junctions (direct cell-cell contacts) interconnect the cells or compartments is unclear. Here I show innexins (which form hemichannels and gap junctions in invertebrates) are abundantly expressed in antennae of adult flies.


I discover innexin-specific patterns of expression and localization, with a majority strongly localizing to glial and other non-neuronal cells, shown with immunostaining and bioinformatic analyses. In a neuron backfilling (dye coupling) case study, I show no such interconnection exists on sensory neurons, implying that such channels are likely exclusive to non-neuronal cells. Based on these observations, I discuss how coupling of sensillum microenvironments or compartments may facilitate odor sensing as well as sensillum homeostasis.
















 





Modulation of the NO‑cGMP pathway has no effect on olfactory responses in the Drosophila antenna.


Prelic et al.


Published in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2023.


Link Supplementary data








NoteSummary(Research Article: 24 pages, 6 figures, 5 supplementary figures)






Nitric oxide (NO) signaling is a ubiquitous mechanism by which cells activity may be potentiated. Here, I use optical and electrophysiological techniques in live antennal tissue to investigate whether NO signaling functions in the olfactory organs of insects. I first demonstrate the presence of NO signaling machinery in antennal tissue. Next, by applying various modulators of the NO-cGMP pathway in open tissue, I show that olfactory responses are unaffected by a wide panel of inhibitors and activators of this pathway, over short and long timescales. This is contrary to expectations, as insect olfactory receptors have been shown to be modulated by cGMP in vitro.


I then examine the action of the cyclic nucleotide family of messengers, previously shown to modulate olfactory receptor functionality, and find that - contrary to expectation - various kinds of applications of cGMP have no effect on olfactory responses in vivo in microinjection, calcium imaging and single sensillum recording experiments. This is differentiated from cAMP effects which confer effects on neuron responses.


In living animals, NO signals may play no role as regulators of olfactory transduction in insects, though may play other physiological roles in insect sensory organs. Several explanations and hypotheses are posed.
















 





Functional interaction between Drosophila olfactory sensory neurons and their support cells.


Prelic et al.


Published in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2022.


Link Supplementary data (EDMOND)








NoteSummary(Research Article: 23 pages, 6 figures, 5 supplementary figures)






Abstract: Insects detect volatile chemicals using antennae, which house a vast variety of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) that innervate hair-like structures called sensilla where odor detection takes place. In addition to OSNs, the antenna also hosts various support cell types. These include the triad of trichogen, tormogen, and thecogen support cells that lie adjacent to their respective OSNs. The arrangement of OSN supporting cells occurs stereotypically for all sensilla and is widely conserved in evolution. While insect chemosensory neurons have received considerable attention, little is known about the functional significance of the cells that support them. For instance, it remains unknown whether support cells play an active role in odor detection, or only passively contribute to homeostasis, e.g., by maintaining sensillum lymph composition. To investigate the functional interaction between OSNs and support cells, we used optical and electrophysiological approaches in Drosophila.


First, we characterized the distribution of various supporting cells using genetic markers. By means of an ex vivo antennal preparation and genetically-encoded Ca2+ and K+ indicators, we then studied the activation of these auxiliary cells during odor presentation in adult flies. We observed acute responses and distinct differences in Ca+ and K+ fluxes between support cell types. Finally, we observed alterations in OSN responses upon thecogen cell ablation in mature adults. Upon inducible ablation of thecogen cells, we notice a gain in mechanical responsiveness to mechanical stimulations during single-sensillum recording, but a lack of change to the neuronal resting activity. Taken together, these results demonstrate that support cells play a more active and responsive role during odor processing than previously thought. Our observations thus reveal that support cells functionally interact with OSNs and may be important for the extraordinary ability of insect olfactory systems to dynamically and sensitively discriminate between odors in the turbulent sensory landscape of insect flight.











As supporting author:





Mokry et al. (2014). Epigenetic regulation of immune tolerance in intestinal epithelium. Journal of Crohn’s and Colitis. DOI link.


Meddens et al. (2019). Stem cells are the principal intestinal epithelial responders to bacterial antigens. SSRN Electronic Journal: Cell Stem Cell. DOI link.








NoteSummary(Research assistance)






I was involved in initial stages performing exploratory qRT-PCR experiments establishing the research story basis, and assisted in proofing first drafts of the paper. The work was delayed as it went through several lead author changes.


My results showed relative changes in mRNA expression of inflammatory markers in intestinal (duodenum, ileum and colon) samples following bacterial antigen exposure. This result served as springboard for further investigations demonstrating that intestinal stem cells (in contrast to enterocytes) are local immune response mediators in the large intestinal epithelium, involving the WNT pathway.


The complete work was eventually published many years later here.

Poster example





A showcase of experimental results from 2021 involving live Ca2+ imaging and custom K+ imaging of both neuronal and non-neuronal cell activity during sensory (odor) stimulation, and electrophysiological recordings of sensory responses in flies where olfactory support cells are intact or absent. This was achieved via cell type-targeted, heat-induced ablation using the GAL4/UAS binary expression system, post-developmentally, to control for complex confoundments.




In 2019, at the Annual Institute Symposium of the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology, I presented a poster entitled Revealing fine details in olfactory sensilla: single-nucleus RNA-seq and the role of support cells in olfaction, showcasing experimental results involving the first-ever single-cell transcriptomic dataset of an insect antenna I made using nuclei isolated from Drosophila melanogaster, and sequenced using the microfluidic droplet-based 10XGenomics platform. The poster also included neuron backfilling and dye tracing results, revealing ultrastructures in insect sensilla newly observed with confocal fluorescence imaging.
